As someone who's actually undergone trauma processing therapy before, yeah, I knew where this was going from the start...
If you look closer on the final erase switch, it says erase all life, meaning a much more less than pleasant ending than memory loss.

What stood out to me most is how Subliminal uses horror to make memory readable. The monster is scary, but the real tension seems to come from how the game visualizes avoidance, suppression, rumination, and confrontation. That makes the horror feel more personal than “mascot chases player.” It’s not only about asking what happened; it’s about asking how someone processes what happened. From a CtrlAble perspective, I think that matters because emotional readability is part of design too. Players need enough clues to understand the fear without the game overexplaining it. The black goo, blocked paths, erased objects, and distorted childhood spaces all communicate mental friction in a way that feels systemic, not just decorative. The strongest point here is that “facing trauma” and “dwelling on trauma” are not treated as the same thing. That distinction makes the story feel a lot more thoughtful. Curious how others see it: do you think mascot horror is strongest when the monster is the threat, or when the monster represents something the character refuses to face?

Lore theory! This is based off of the song Qwel posted as well as the lore room video. (Both of which are canon)

 In dandy’s world, the seasonal room has a secret room in the side. In there is a video tape where Delilah tells Cocoa that Bassie is feeling “unwell” just as she expected. Delilah instructs cocoa to give Bassie a gift for her, and when cocoa agrees Delilah gives her the whispering flower. The tape cuts off after this but we do learn a few things. My theory is that the whispering flower took over Bassie, and here’s why. In this song we see that Bassie doesn’t want to hurt cocoa, she hugs her and writes I’m sorry all over the wall, but she also writes “get her” too. Why on earth would she attack her if she felt sorry? A few of you noticed that she closed her “conscious” eye when attacking cocoa, and she also yells  “Get her!” While another part of her says “What?” Here’s where my theory resides. The whispering flower was given to Bassie by cocoa before she became twisted, as the song shows Bassie looking at the flower near the start. The flower might have been filling her head with more doubt and insecurities, using her jealousy of cocoa to get at Bassie’s weak points, hence the “whispering” flower part. The flower eventually took over Bassie when she was at her most vulnerable. I don’t know about you, but Bassie’s twisted arm, where it meets the shoulder, has a flower sprouting there, and nowhere else, I think it looks exactly like the whispering flower, and the eye of the flower sprouted into the horrendous arm. The flower is now apart of her consciousness, forcing her to attack cocoa, while her other side, Bassie, writes sorry and says “What?” In protest. Obviously, she can’t do much, the flower is too powerful, forcing Bassie’s eye closed in order to complete this task. One more thing, this also is a deeper reason as to why the whispering flower says “She deserves it!” As cocoa was the one who gave Bassie the flower, and is the reason Bassie isn’t herself anymore. Also, the song and lyrics perfectly match my theory. She says "I'm not wilting I'm just what they made" over and over again, and I think that's the whispering flower speaking in her thoughts, because the whispering flower is just what Delilah made. Also, baskets don't wilt, flowers do, which is why they may have chosen wilting as the name of the song instead of anything else. (I thought it was strange they chose wilting of all names) In the beginning, she is standing in a field of flowers, and is clearly having a nightmare about the whispering flower. Although it doesn't seem like it, the whispering flower was telling Bassie to be just like Cocoa, and when Bassie woke up, she was terrified. In the end she also says it's too late to save me, meaning it's too late to save her from the flower.

If you find any flaws in this please tell me, and if you have any theories also tell me them as well.
Apologies for any spelling or revising errors.

I feel like Rich would be too old to be the player, so what if he is instead the one the player is looking for? What if the player isn't Rich, but the young employee Rich called "Kid"?
The player being the "Kid" actually fits weirdly well and explains a lot of things. We barely know anything about the "Kid", the fact that he doesn't get a name at all being odd in itself. But what we do know is that he is a lot like how Rich once was, someone willing to speak out. Which Rich noticed and made him look out for this "kid", almost in a father-like way. There is clearly a bond there, and I think that is important. 
The Kid wouldn't have been involved with the experiments, but he could've still seen or heard something he shouldn't have. The guilt doesn't have to come from direct involvement; it could also have come from not saying anything about it for years. 
I think there is a reason why the player keeps getting asked about his reasons for coming here after all these years. If the player knew everything, why bother looking for clues and watching tapes? If the player is Rich, why would he watch his own tapes? Sure, it could be game logic. But what if the reason is that the player wants to find out what happened to Rich? 
If the Kid had a close bond with Rich, it explains why we hear about him in every chapter. What became of Rich could be the answer the player is looking for, as it could have been something the Kid had wondered for years. 
As for why the Kid wasn't there during the Hour of Joy, what if he originally did have a shift that day but got a call from Rich telling him not to come?
Rich could've had a bad feeling about the plan to release the toys, and didn't want the young employee he had formed a bond with to be there just in case it went bad. Basically saving the Kid from The Hour of Joy, which would eventually result in the Kid coming back for the events of the Game and finally putting an end to things. 
I feel like the player being the Kid not only adds up, but also works really well for the story. Rich is a character you easily grow to like. Therefore getting a final tape from him where he leaves a final message directly to the player could actually hit emotionally. 
I could go more in-depth, but I don't want to go on for too long. 
To sum it up: I think the Player is the "Kid" Rich talks to, and that he came back to find out what happened to Rich.

58:44 btw, about Brahm's lullaby, though I assume the theorists know this: the German text of it is a bit disturbing. Especially the last couplet of the first verse. In German, it says "Morgen früh, wenn Gott will, wirst du wieder geweckt", which would translate as "Tomorrow morning, if God wants it, you'll be woken up again". (Or rather "if it's God's will", that would be more elegant of a translation, but I tried to stay as close to the German text as possible.) While it probably read as very normal back then - strong displays of submission/subservience to God's will were very common back then as far as I know - the modern interpretation is more sinister; it reminds us that we may not wake up again tomorrow, that we can die at any moment, even while we sleep. In the context of the entire theory, I suppose it could be Fiona (Mimic 1) sort of pleading with Edwin to not destroy Mimic 2. To let him 'wake up again' the next morning. It would also mean that Fiona is likening Edwin to God, which, given he created the Mimics, is probably not too far off. But yeah. 
Don't know why the official English version is "Lay thee down and rest, may thy slumber be blessed". Similar meaning, but loses the edge, in my opinion.

A little rant, sorry:

As a full on "Gardener" writer, I absolutely understand Scott. I had an outcome and an ending outlined for my story, I just didn't know how my characters would get to it. But as the story progressed, that ending didn't fit no matter how hard I tried to force it. Sometimes you have to let the story go the way it wants to, because otherwise it will wither and become something you hate, instead of your passion, just like a real garden. If you try to force a sunflower to be something different (e.g. you try to make the yellow petals turn blue), it won't work no matter what, and you will simply grow frustrated and abandon the garden all together.

Sometimes you just have to leave a plant alone and unattended for it to grow to its full height. Sometimes you have to leave a plotpoint alone and unattended for it to grow into what you need down the line.
Maybe one day, the box will finally give Scott an answer. Maybe it will grow into something actually needed for the story. Maybe it will suddenly give Scott an opportunity to tie in a dead-end he hits. Maybe it won't. Maybe the flower will never take good enough roots to grow to its full potential. And that's okay, that's how writting sometimes is and we shouldn't be mad at him. It's not like with books, where the writer can go back a chapter to edit it. Each game is a chapter that's published independently and cannot be edited.

Sometimes a Flower dies and nothing can be done about it. You just have to honor it and plant another one.

I once heard a writing advice that can apply to this perfectly: "The key to write good foreshadowing is to be vague enough that whatever you come up with fits perfectly".

Is ok to not know what you'll do, you can have an idea of where a plot is going to lead, or have it all figured out. But if the characters lead you elsewhere you need to have room to pivot and course correct properly. This is why vagueness helps, it gives you the wiggle room AND makes readers wonder about what it could mean.

Not paying off this "set up" is bad because it just leaves the writer and the audience unsatisfied.

It felt like something where I could pull my own personal experience and knowledge to relate to. Thanks for addressing the ideas of storytelling in video games!

Speaking as a gardener-style writer myself, it is VITAL to at least have some sense of where your story is going when you start writing it - you can't build up to something if you don't know what you're building up to, you can't nurture a seed into blooming if you don't even know what kind of seed it is. Knowing your endpoint is almost more important than knowing your starting point; whether or not you know any of the other points that will happen along the way depends on how you personally craft stories, but you need AN ending in mind before you start. And maybe, on the way to that ending, you'll change your mind about what it should be, it's good to keep your options open; but if you just have no clue where you're going at all, your story WILL fall apart. While I often find myself making connections in stories I'm in the process of writing that I myself didn't see until I theorized about my own story, and I take joy in those moments, in order to build up to something, you have to at least have SOME awareness of it from the start. The fact that Scott presented the box to his audience before he'd fully developed what was inside it has never sat right with me - it's good to let plot points develop naturally during the writing process, but don't show them off to your audience before you know what they are. To me, the box is a cautionary tale not to take your own art for granted; always put in the work BEFORE you share your creation.

Something that was missed in the “what we got right” segment: Chicken Scratch, the possum, was Jordan Cook. As he bonds with Amanda in the tapes (much to Wooly’s ire), his jabbering becomes slightly more understandable. At the beginning of the healthy-eating tape, when Amanda and Wooly are making their introductions, Chicken Scratch pops up from behind the counter between them wearing a toque and shouts, “AHN AHM JOHR DUN!” before Amanda dubs him Chicken Scratch, due to his speech sounding like the audible version of illegible handwriting, or “chicken-scratch”. Johr Dun = Jordan, plus the toque (a hat commonly worn by chefs, or cooks), Jordan Cook.

Side note: Chicken Scratch’s name has a deeper meaning, at least to Amanda. What animal is most associated with Sam across the chapters? Funny Mr. Rooster, a chicken. Rebecca is showing how much she’s liking Jordan by giving him a name that also symbolizes someone else she deeply cares for. And one way you as the player can jump-start that connection, fun fact, is during the candy tape where Chicken-Scratch spawns in. When Amanda asks what you do to cheer up a friend who is sad, if you answer “hug”, she laments how long it’s been since someone’s hugged her. Promptly, Chicken Scratch will hug her, sympathizing with her, and Amanda will return the gesture. 💔🥲

I noticed something when I was rewatching the older Amanda tapes, and I’m honestly shocked nobody has pointed it out yet to my knowledge.

So after finishing the newest game, I went back to the first game—the episode with the dead fox. And suddenly something clicked. In the new game, we see Amanda’s dad sneaking out to go see her, and he ends up getting killed by the demon. Now keep that in mind.

Look at the fox scene again:
	•	The fox sneaks out → trying to get the sweet berries
	•	The bear trap snaps and kills it

Now compare:
	•	Amanda’s dad sneaks out → trying to reach her
	•	The demon kills him

The symbolism lines up way too perfectly.
Fox = Amanda’s dad
Berries = Amanda
Trap = the demon 

And what’s even more interesting is the way Amanda talks about the fox. It sounds almost like she’s explaining something she doesn’t fully understand, like she’s unconsciously telling us what happened to her father without saying it directly.

I’m starting to think Amanda has been dropping hints like this from the beginning. She might not consciously remember everything, but her subconscious does, and it leaks into the tapes.

Like the hospital scene — that could easily be her trying to show us something from her past. I feel like there are more moments like this if we go back and rewatch everything carefully.

Anyway, this is just something I noticed, and I can’t tell if I’m the only one who sees the connection. If anyone else picked up on this, let me know.

The bubbling goo and the illustration of the “5” instantly reminded me of cell-culture work, specifically immortalized cell lines like HeLa cells. There’s actually a wild real-world story behind those: HeLa cells are cancer cells taken (without her consent) from a woman named Henrietta Lacks in 1951. They’ve been growing in labs for over 70 years, and scientists estimate that more than 50 million metric tons of them exist today.

What makes them so heavily used is exactly what makes them eerie: as long as you give them nutrients, they grow indefinitely—and they spread everywhere. They’re used in all kinds of experiments, from basic biology to tissue engineering and attempts at regenerating artificial organs. With the right growth factors or special media (some mimicking elements found in amniotic fluid), you can push them to mimic certain cell types… though this often leads to tumors instead of proper tissues.

Interestingly, HeLa lines are cataloged using letter-and-number combinations—kind of like the naming conventions you’d expect in a lab making… well… giant toys.

So it’s not hard to imagine something similar happening in Poppy Playtime: immortalized cancer-like cells could easily be the “secret ingredient” behind Bigger Bodies and the other experiments. It would explain why Poppy is so unique—maybe her biology lets her survive the cellular chaos without developing uncontrollable cancer.

The one thing that still doesn’t line up, though, is how she survives without food or water. Even immortal cells need nutrients—unless there’s something paranormal (or scientifically very questionable) filling in the gaps.

I think you missed something entirely.
SEGA recognised that the timeline and lore of Sonic has been all over the place and doesn't fit together well in some areas, and other areas are left in limbo as to whether or not they're cannon. As of about 2 years back they officially formed a small lore team comprising of various knowledgeable individuals at SEGA, including some of the game and comic writers, to work through the whole of Sonic history and make a single cohesive lore that would fix continuity, but also give them a basis and direction for future titles. This included working out the order of some stories, the importance of others, how some connect together, and more importantly what was to be considered cannon and what was not. This is why a lot of titles are missing from the timeline, as they are not considered cannon anymore.

It should also be noted that this is an ongoing project too, and the currently present timeline is a work in progress.

And as a side note, it's not just the games, the current IDW comics have now been drafted in as cannon also.

I’ve also seen fashion students who embroider a special pattern onto their completed garments that, when seen from the right angle, becomes their name. The signatures help the artist/creator to outlive themselves, which is how we still discuss artists like Van Gogh or Brahms long after they’ve passed away. I am a programmer, and I have worked on games. Interpreting "X-form" as "transform" is reasonable, but the rest of the interpretation is a big stretch. There really isn't anything pushing towards interpreting the word as referring to coordinate transformations (which is what game transforms ultimately are), there's nothing pushing towards interpreting the coordinate transformations as hierarchical, and "parent/child" in the context of hierarchies is a metaphor which will pretty much never reflect a more literal parent child relationship. If two game characters are parent and child, their game objects will almost never have a parent/child coordinate relationship.

As a therapist in school to be a doctor of psychology, I believe this shift is because the developers themselves are opening up from generations of repression around certain subjects, specifically, openly discussing trauma and mental health; something the previous generations didn't want to do because it was taboo to talk about trauma, or it was greatly toned-down and santitzed before discussing it.

Now the developers the means, and psychological and emotional growth, to convey both trauma and mental health as it is. 

And for we, as the viewers and consumers,  who come from trauma, its cathartic to see and play through games that not only validate the trauma many of us have been gaslit into believing that our trauma doesnt matter (and typically the ones telling us this are the abusive ones who perpetuate it to keep from taking accountability), but its also giving us an interactive medium (video games) that portrays said trauma (and lasting effects) in a way that is real, if oftentimes, difficultly disgestable.

One note I'd like to throw out there about the "kid friendly horror phase":

DDLC flew under the radar in part because, somehow, in the West, anime is still perceived as "for kids", because "it's a cartoon, and cartoons are for kids" (cartoons were not for kids originally, even in the West). Add to that the absolute sea of cringey dating sims, there was a perfect setup to pull the rug out from everyone who didn't read the description. If ad company execs had watched stuff like Evangelion, Outlaw Star, and the like back around the turn of the millennium, DDLC would not have been able to sneak by as "kid friendly". Sure, anime is visually appealing and very expressive... but I've been got enough to know that when it goes dark, those expressions do great work in conveying some of the darkest moments anyone can experience.
Animation is a medium, not an age range.

@The Game Theorists I tried to say this in chat, but in the game, 4625 is a frequency that Edwin sets the basement audio log to in order to hear something that sounds like Fiona. In real life, 4625 kHz is the frequency used for UVB-76, AKA "The Buzzer". It is known to make a continuous buzzing sound, but occasionally, it will repeat a message (in this case, some message in Russian). This seems very similar to what we hear when Edwin tries to contact the voice on the radio.

I dont think that the supernatural aspect has to be removed or retconned at all, and infact, it does seem like there is some sort of paranormal activity that happened following Fiona's death and what prompted Edwin to make the Mimic and the M1 program in the first place. When we find the secret room in the White Tiger section, the audio recording available indicates that, after Fiona's death, Edwin while in this same area, had heard her voice. We also learn that Edwin isn't sure how the Mimic and M1 work at all, he has no idea how he got the two to function in the first place and appears incapable of replicating them, despite the clear attempts to make a second Mimic endo. During that same White Tiger section, the White Tiger itself stands alone when compared to everything else we encounter in the game. Sure the Mimic can quickly swap bodies without us being able to see it do so, but no matter what other shell it is wearing, the one thing we never see it do is teleport while wearing a suit. Thats what sets the White Tiger apart, you could be walking down one path and then suddenly the Tiger spawns in front of you, and its not a case of it already being there in the dark and suddenly becoming visible from the Star Orphan light, we can actively see the whole suit just POOF into existence. It could be argued that by this point Arnold is so tired from being awake for 36+ hours that he is starting to hallucinate, which can happen starting after more than 24 hours of wakefulness, but why would he start hallucinating the White Tiger? Up until this point in the game, Arnold has had almost no opportunities to see the Tiger at all for his brain to start hallucinating it. It just makes much more sense for it to be a paranormal event, rather than the Mimic in the suit. We also need to take into account the Tiger's behavior. It stands there. When it spawns in, all it does is stand there menacingly, but it never moves to actively chase Arnold, not until the section where the lights begin going out and we have to run from one light to the next, and even then it wont attack until it has caught us in the dark. The Mimic hasn't operated in that way at all through the whole game, and has instead relentlessly and actively hunted us, running towards us the moment it sees us or the moment it hears something, but it has never stood there menacingly just staring. 

So, my own personally theory as to why M1 worked in the first place is that Fiona's spirit was able to actually inhabit the Mimic endo and the self learning AI system the endo had. After David's death, Edwin attempted to make a second endo but failed, and instead, with Fiona's encouragement, removed her AI and placed it in the F10 N4 computer, and attempted to teach the new program in the Mimic endo, M2, to be David. This attempt failed though because, unlike M1, David's soul hadn't attached itself to the AI like Fiona's had, and instead got lost beneath the MCM, eventually manifesting as the White Tiger, his favorite toy.

Like, Elliot is related to Xipe Totec, and Elliot represents Simon. Sarah, having a dead twin, represents Quetzalcoatl. Debbie, being the "sorcerer" and the "enemy", needs to be Tezcatlipoca. That means that Terry represents Huitzilpotchtli, the god of sun, war and fire. We have four main characters which potentially correlate to the four Tezcatlipocas (5 if we include Sarah's dead twin, representing Xolotol). *Although* it might be that Terry, or Mr T, is actually Tezcatlipoca, while Debbie is Huitzilpotchtli.

If the ARG would give us 6(7) characters it would actually be much better for this theory- we have 4 Tezcatlipocas, Tlaloc and his wife who represent 2 of the 5 suns, and Xolotol, and might even include representation of Huitzilpotchtli's sister and enemy the moon goddess, but as it stands, the 4 Tezcatlipocas work well to describe the story as is

Hi, chemist here who works with nitrogen gases almost daily, when in equilibrium with nitrogen dioxide, Nitrogen tetroxide is a colorless gas. However, when at room temp, nitrogen tetroxide is far more unstable, and the equilibrium will shift towards nitrogen dioxide. The tanks in the basement are almost certainly used for preservation rather than poisoning. The symptoms described align with most gasses, meaning that the identity of the gas probably doesn’t matter. There is also the fact that nitrogen tetroxide reacts with water in the air to form both nitrous and nitric acid, which are both a liquid.

Grass hay, like Western Orchard Grass weighs on the lighter side and is about 70-90 pounds, and is much more enjoyable to pick up. 

Also I noticed this too. There are only 2 strings on the hay bale which yes, in real life, there are 2 string bales, but those are pretty small. The larger bales are 3 stringed, and the biggest bales use 6-8 strings. Usually when organizing hay bales, it’s stacked by a 2x6 on the 1st layer, then a 2x4 on the 2nd layer, and you keep doing that. Easier for the Squeeze to transport (the designed forklift that is specialized in hay loading).

Fun fact, the pikmin are canonically part of a taxonomical class called "Ambuloradicis" (walking root). They share this class with the Creeping Chrysanthemum, a plant-animal hybrid enemy. There's a variant of the Creeping Chrysanthemum that boasts a fungal appearance rather than a floral one, and it's called the Startle Spore. It's a parasite that has chosen a group of mushrooms as its host, and Olimar compares it to the Bulbmin, a Pikmin species that parasitizes Bulborbs.

For your force calculation on the heavy armor, you're assuming that the entire moment of acceleration is coming from the blade's deployment. But if you look at the attack, that isn't what happens. There are three things taking place simultaneously: the blade is deploying, the right arm is moving in to deliver the strike, and the left arm is pulling the target backwards into the strike. Additionally, while the animation doesn't differ on an armored target, it's safe to assume that the assassin would be aiming for a joint in the armor or a spot between plates, such as around the neck. All of this is to say that if a skilled assassin is able to get that close to a target, the armor likely won't save them.

So, tiny theory on the identity of the player. We all know they used to work at Playtime Co, but GT has been assuming you're playing as one of the higher-ups who came back. I'm very confident that's no longer the case. One person I absolutely know we're not if Leith Pierre, since we wouldn't have fallen for our own tape trap.

One of the secret tapes has a floor manager, Rick, discuss the behavior of a bad employee with said employee. He's simply addressed as "Kid" in the subtitles for the tape, and he's called in for getting angry at other employees teasing using the various horrifying rumors around Playtime Co. He's frustrated, but seems to be pretty firmly in the dark about what's actually going on. Rick seems to be on his side, trying to protect him from getting in trouble and possibly turned into a toy.

Maybe Rick pulled some strings and had "Kid" either fired after repeated issues (instead of being experimented on, a very nice thing to do) or cut his hours so he wasn't at Playtime Co during the Hour of Joy. I'm not 100% saying the player character is the Kid from the secret tape, but I think it's for more likely we're playing as someone like them rather than a higher-up. A grunt worker disturbed by all the horrifying rumors and curiosity - as well as perhaps some second-hand guilt - finally got the better of them.

The issue I have with the comparison between the novels and the newer books is that the two are ENTIRELY different in context. 
The original novels are purposefuly made to be their own timeline and it's clear, because we see each event happen or hear about each event from the beginning to the end of its timeline. 
The fnaf novels are their own stories with narrative arcs, a clear timeline, and without any holes.


On the other hand, fazbear fright books are snippets of a timeline with no context to fill in the gap. We skip from TMIR1280 to the stichwraith epilogues to frailty to afton's amalgamation death WITHOUT anything in between. 
The truth is, we obsessed so much about knowing if these books are canon to the games that we forgot to ask if the games are canon to these books. Because THEY ARE. Without the events FROM THE GAMES, 1:1, the fright universe makes no sense. Without FFPS and UCN, the epilogues don't make any sense. What happened to that ancient fire site and the owners of fazbear's? The books don't tell- the games do. 
What is springtrap and why is there a corpse inside of it? The books never tell. The games do.

Where in the trilogy of novels, each character is explained and rationalized and shown, in the newer books, you need to know what happens in the games to know why the books happen. 
And if the games are canon to the books, then the books are canon to the games.

Another thing to note, the neighbours bricking up Poppy’s home is reminiscent of “The Cask of Amontillado”,  a short story by Edgar Allan Poe, the same person who wrote “The Telltale Heart”, the story the neighbours were performing. 

For those unaware, “The Cask of Amontillado” is about a man who lured his drunken friend to the wine cellar, only to then chain him up and brick him up behind a wall. Whereas “The Telltale Heart” is about someone who killed his roommate under the conviction that he was evil, buried his body under the floorboards, but was then haunted/driven crazy by the sounds of his roommate’s beating heart only they could hear. 

I'm not sure how this ties into the story of “Welcome Home”,  but I think it's noteworthy to mention.

It's nice to have a concise collection of everything we know about this series! While I'm here, I just wanted to note down some things I noticed about the read-along video:

- It's weird how Sally is sorta made to feel guilty and inconsiderate for asking Poppy to join the play. It may be common knowledge that Poppy didn't like scary things, but I think the idea of Sally simply asking her if she wanted to join being this rude and awful thing was a bit of an overreaction. After all, Sally relented to Poppy's apprehension in the end, and Poppy herself didn't seem to feel upset or railroaded in her responses. This to me is another subtle indication of the indoctrination of the neighborhood, where those specifically seeking closer bonds or in some way opposing Home's influence is reprimanded systematically. Seems another attempt by Home to further ostracize the neighbors from each other slowly and quietly, like picking the wings off a butterfly.


- It was also a bit jarring how the neighbors immediately decided to go to the extreme and brick up Poppy's windows without even asking her first. Given how Sally felt about possibly hurting her friend, one would think she and the others would at least visit Poppy directly and suggest bricking her windows, but no....they just go onto her property and tamper with it. The idea of not respecting a person's boundaries and making decisions for them is also a common thing seen within most cult practices, as it takes away a person's individuality and dehumanizes them. We've already seen this occur with Eddie Dear, and now it's happening to Poppy.

- A bit of a lighter observation, but notice that the first characters Home tries to take control of (after Wally that is) are known to be particularly large in size. Sorta feels like the classic tactic of taking out the largest opponents first so the weakest members of a group are left defenseless.

- Adding onto the last observation: I find it intriguing that the two characters who are present when Poppy and Eddie are snapped out of Home's control are Sally and Frank. We already know Frank's significance, but what of Sally? Maybe she two will become aware of Home's indoctrination? Maybe she's a bit more open to the clues around her because she doesn't even come from earth as a literal shooting star!

Not sure if anyone pointed this out, but using the name “Coppelia” for his daughter is really interesting. Coppelia was the original robot kid.

It comes from the ballet Coppelia which features a young man falling in love with a strange woman called Coppelia. Eventually, it’s revealed that she’s actually a doll. The inventor that made her wants her to come to life and tries to use magic to steal the young man’s soul. It’s based on Der Sandmann by ETA Hoffmann. The whole point is that she’s indistinguishable from a real human which really feels like a point for the “Robot Kid” theories from this franchise.

It’s a really clever Easter egg if nothing else!

You can't use the amount pay as a way to gauge the year, employers don't pay you the amount of hours you worked that week, but the previous week. So if the security guard is getting paid $120.50 on the week they're working their first full week, then the previous week could have been orientation and training pay. So the new guard could have been paid for 4 hours of orientation one day, then 8 hours of training for a total of 12 hours if the guard is getting paid $10 an hour, and most places pay a night shift premium as well. Then there's states that have their own minimum wage, and there's places that pay more than minimum wage. There's way too many factors that go into how much the security guard is getting paid to make an accurate call on the year if you're going to use minimum wage.

9:50 “Who watches the watcher” is not originally from Star Trek. It is actually a phrase in Latin (“Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?”) that the Romans used to refer to the guards men would hire to ensure their wives would not cheat on them when they were away because the guards, inevitably, were the ones the wives cheated with. It eventually became a phrase used as a critique of those in positions of power through Plato’s “Republic”. It is also commonly used in the Watchmen comics, which began in 1987, and is what the name of the comic is derived from.

Edit: All I mean by this is that the line is not necessarily a reference to 1989 media. This specific translation (using “watchers” rather than “watchmen” or “guardsmen,” which are much more common in comparison) could indicate that the intention was to reference Star Trek. However, it could instead (or perhaps additionally) be more thematic, it could be an inadvertent commentary on William’s actions, as parents rely on him to make the experience for their children safe when he is in fact the one harming them himself. It could also be a 1987 media reference to the aforementioned Watchmen comics, which is one of the first pieces of pop culture to use the phrase. The only piece of pop culture from before Watchmen that Wikipedia lists as referencing the phrase is the song “Justice” by The Pop Group. “Guards! Guards!,” the eighth Discworld book, also references this line and is also from 1989, though that is an erroneous version of the original Latin phrase (“Quis custodiet custard?”). All this to say that I do not believe this line is good evidence to support the idea that the game takes place in 1989, as the true origin and potential references it could be part of are too varied and the purpose of the line could very well be something else entirely.

"Who Watches The Watchers" is an interesting pick from Scott, when it comes to Star Trek episodes:

The episode is about a group of scientists who were observing an alien race that were only in the bronze age. They were observing them using holograms to mask their presence, but the technology failed due to an accident. The Enterprise came to aid the science team, but one of the aliens noticed the research site, and got injured due to the malfunctioning technology. Since the alien's injuries were their fault, they healed his injuries and attempted to erase his memories of the encounter. Instead, the alien remembered the entire encounter, and thought that Captain Picard was a God who used his magic to heal his injuries, prompting him to tell his village that he's met God. Now with a belief system, the aliens start doing things that they think will appease their God, including trying to sacrifice someone who supposedly disobeyed their God.

The episode works as two cautionary tales. The first one is the importance of not interfering in underdeveloped cultures, and the unintended consequences that could accompany said actions. The second lesson is the importance to not blindly serve one you believe is your deity, as you might gravely misinterpret their will, or their intent.

It's interesting how Scott's known for being a religious man, and that he'd reference an episode of a show that would show religion in a negative light.

I have a few concerns with the theory. For one, when you listen to the doctor scene, you hear a voice that sounds just like Woolley chase off the camera operator. If Woolley and Sam are one and the same, you either wouldn’t have heard a voice, or would have heard Sam’s. Beyond that, in the final episode in the alley, you can mention Sam. When you do, Amanda states that “he was too trusting.” That seems to contradict the hypothesis that Rebecca thinks Sam abandoned her. Then there are multiple times in the game where you can type Woolley or Sam, and the responses are very different. Sure that could mean that she doesn’t know they are one and the same, but it feels like the creators are trying to draw a clear line between them. Then with the blue tape, we see that Hameln is reinterpreting his words and are unable to make him say the statement outright. If that’s the case, it feels unsatisfying to say that he gave in anyways. Then with the “I can’t take this anymore” line, it feels like Woolley is fed up with Amanda, that contradicts Sam’s characterization of being dedicated to Rebecca with everything he has. He sounds sick dealing with her, and that just doesn’t seem right. At the moment, it feels like the devs want us to keep guessing who Woolley is. It doesn’t feel conclusive. While the arguments make sense for both, I can’t feel satisfied with that when Woolley contradicts Sam’s characterization.

Dave might have replied with "I'm scared" for a multitude of reasons. He may have said this because when he does dream, if at all, he only has nightmares that make him terrified. Now that question reads as "Do you have dreams?" and the response means "Yes, and I'm scared of them". Dave could have also replied with "I'm scared" because he is scared to see what would happen if he tries to dream. Think about it, if Dave is the protagonist of the FNAF 4 game, he probably doesn't feel safe trying to sleep after that traumatic experience, especially for a little kid. With this in mind, the question reads "Do you have dreams?" and the response means "I'm scared of dreams" or "I'm scared to try and dream" or "I'm scared of falling asleep". There are many other ways this two word response can be interpreted with or without the context of the Nightmare picture, but those are the ones that make the most sense to me. Einstein's math allows for negative mass.  It's the main reason theories about white holes and anti-universes exist.  With math, however, you aren't constrained by the laws of physics in the same way we are.  The equations work with both positive and negative values.  This proves that anti-gravity can mathematically exist, but it's likely not something that can exist in practice.  It's the same thing with Einstein-Rosen Bridges (Wormholes).  They can exist mathematically, but likely not in practice.  At least not for long enough to actually utilize them, since they collapse before even light can get through fully.  But we used to think black holes were impossible despite the math allowing it, so who knows what's really out there?

A couple things wrong in this video. 

First, when you calculate the mass using density and volume, you get 329.8 kg which is mass, but then you equate it to 727 lbs which is a weight, not a mass. The correct equivalence would be 22.5 Slug which is the imperial mass unit, which when multiplied by Minecraft gravity in imperial units (104.9 ft/s^2) you get over 2300 lbs of weight, so I’m not sure where the 727 lbs is coming from. 

Secondly, the F=ma calculate that you perform to find the impact force is actually just a weight calculation. 10,553.6 N is equal to 2,372 lbs, which is the weight I showed earlier. Weight vs impact force is very different. Having a 10 lb dumbbell rest on your chest is very different than having one thrown at you. 

You need to use the work-energy principle to find the impact force, not F=ma. The work-energy principle states that the change in kinetic energy is equal to the work done during impact. So you can say: Force x distance traveled = change in KE. The change in KE is just the Potential Energy, and the distance is the theoretical amount of distance Steve would travel after the fall (e.g. if he creates a crater in the ground it would be a block or two). The more distance Steve travels after the impact, the less impact force there is (same principle with cars and crumple zones to increase travel distance in a crash). 

So the final equation to find the impact force would be F = mgh/d where m is the mass of Steve, g is the acceleration due to gravity, h is the height he fell from, and d is the distance he travels (vertically) after impact. The final answer should be much higher than what was calculated.

Just a handy tidbit of info regarding Carbon Steel: the "monsters" in that game are actually animals that've been immensely warped by the intense pressures of the depths to the point of unrecognizability. The "execs" within the game stated that they were doing experiments to see how subterranean pressures cause severe mutations on surface-dwelling lifeforms. And if you choose not to try and escape (yes, there is a choice), the guys up top will say that because of your testing expertise, they've decided to make your character the first *human* test subject to undergo this process. Then, you're knocked out by someone from behind, and when you wake up, where are you now? That's right, the *same* test tube that you've been pulling the creatures up with, going through the *same* test of being sedated and having data extracted from you.

A more grounded in reality look at the ending would be that Rocio realized that being online was triggering her old trauma, and bringing out the worst parts of her past. The imagery of her being wrapped in computer cables would be a physical representation of her, feeling trapped by her online life.
Deleting herself, then, would mean abandoning her old life and creating a new identity. But she wasn’t able to let go of the website and the games because she still believes that the message she was trying to convey was important. Those little glimpses of her interacting could be her using the one connection to her past she still has, the website and the games, to see if anything has changed, or wondering about her old friends and using the website to try and check on them. 
I don’t know what’s more tragic, someone so consumed by their trauma that they end up converting themselves into a part of the games they made to try and escape it, or someone that did literally everything they could, including inventing a new identity, to escape their past, and still finding themselves drawn back to it.

Consider the narrator.
Originally, you were given the story through the eyes of Manfred, depicting others the way he saw them.
Now, you're given the story from Nils' perspective, depicting others the way he saw them.
Neither view is "the truth."
"The truth" lies somewhere in between.
Manfred viewed his wife as an obstacle to his progress in resurrecting his daughter, and saw Nils as assisting her in her obstruction.
Nils was separated from Manfred as a boy and had his mother's perspective impressed onto him as he was raised.
He likely only really remembers his sister getting sick, her passing, his father being stricken by grief, and leaving with his mother.
Everything else he "remembers" about the events were stories from his mother, heavily influencing what he *perceives* to be the truth, but is not.
Kind of an extremely obvious thing to overlook, and pretty scummy to accept one unreliable narrator's perspective but disregard the other's as the lies of some monster.
A father desperately tries to make his family whole again after a tragedy befalls them, albeit misguidedly, his wife leaves and takes his remaining child with her, leaving him alone with his grief that turns into resentment before he spirals downward into the darkness.
The son grows up separated from his father, his memories of him slowly replaced with memories of stories of him, and eventually creates a new version of his father's game, altering it to fit *his* perspective and tell the story as he "remembers" it.

A horror ARG that deals with how the "protagonist's" actions affected his remaining family is super cool. I love how Nils isn't driven mad or forced down the same path as his father. Instead he learned from what he did and committed himself to being a better father to his own kids. Also  the fact that he doesn't forgive his father, but he is willing to talk to him?

This whole ARG just feels a lot more mature than other ones I know, and not in the "adult" blood and gore sense, but rather that Nils feels likes a realistic person trying to get over the trauma of his sister's early death and his father's neglect. You could even take the supernatural elements as a metaphor and have the whole thing just be about Nils' journey to accepting the bad things in his childhood and moving on from them.

It's refreshing to have a story with such a mature and, actually, kinda uplifting ending.

To be fair, most tanks have been manufactured with the mindset of, "It should drive like a car or a tractor." It's not something like the old steam tractors where you have 15 levers, one for power, one to release pressure, one to turn left, one to turn right, one to allow you to turn left or right, one to allow you to move the other 14 levers, etc. It's literally throw someone in, pedals be either gas and brake or brake for either side and the tillers act like they would on an old tractor or a steering wheel to act similar to how it does on a car. It will just ride differently from the two, as cars aren't as heavy and tractors don't have a large 75mm cannon sticking out on the top.

While the aspect of application (driving and gunning from gameplay) probably isn't the most direct, the tactics are. There's a very recent anecdote of this from Ukraine about two M2 Bradleys taking on a T-90. One of the Bradley commanders recalled back playing WarThunder and had his gunner aim at the turret ring barrel and vision block of the T-90 as they appear in the game of WarThunder. So was it applicable from the game as far as gameplay to operations? No, not really. Was the tactics translatable? Yeah.

One last part of Minecraft's lore missed out on here is who exactly Steve and/or Alex are. There's one theory I found on Reddit I personally like, and I was surprised MatPat got so close to it but went the zombie path instead.
So this theory is basically that the illagers were trying to bring back the builders from zombies (not counting MatPat's theory around zombies yet), and eventually succeeded in their experiments. They took a zombie and fused it with a totem of undying. By imbuing it with new life, they succeeded in reviving an ancient builder and bringing him back to full consciousness.
But the illagers quickly realized how dangerous this had become. They had an uncontrollable force loose in their base, and he remembered nothing about who they were, attacking them and attempting to escape. They killed him to protect themselves and ended these experiments, realizing how close they had come to destroying themselves.
However, they didn't realize the Totem of Undying had done much more than bring this zombie back to life. It had changed him. Imbued with its power, he had become truly undying. I have one tiny little "criticism" for this list: the frustration management aspect.

As a lot of gamers know, the "gamer rage"TM is something that needs to be kept in check. And if one doesn't get confronted with failure enough times during their journey into learning how to play videogames, they might get frustrated more easily and at lower trigger levels, given that the frustration management is not learned from the start and they don't get desensitized to the frustration aspect of games, such as losing, dying, miscalculating a jump (Witcher 3 fans, represent) or simply having a game crash on them and they didn't save, making them lose progress.
The last point can be overcome with the autosave feature which is now practically omnipresent.

My mom is new to gaming on anything beyond a Wii, and that was several years ago. We have a PS4, and the controller has a LOT of buttons if you're a new gamer. We play Resident Evil 6 together (she loves Resident Evil, and it's co-op. Not a great game, but it's fun lol), so she printed out a diagram of what the buttons do. Which button is run, which is shoot, what the buttons are called, etc. She doesn't usually need it anymore, unless it's been a while since we played, but it was a great reference.

i learned video games through spore, it literally teaches all of these concepts in order, but for keyboard and mouse. you start with just clicking on stuff to either go or attack, then you learn key binds for different attacks, then it incorporates 3d movement without it being too much of a hassle alongside moving the camera, you pretty much never absolutely need to jump, you just can. it demonstrates strategical thinking in the tribal and city stages, while even somewhat simplifying the controls while introducing new ones, and finally fully immersive 3d movement with key bind utility in the space stage. it requires reading only in the city-space stages of the game, you can just explain what to do in place of the tutorial boxes.

 i ended up basically unlocking new areas of the game as i learned to read, i kept replaying it until i thought "hey reading this tutorial for the tribal stage isn't so bad" also halfway through playing spore i learned Minecraft, if you don't want the person you are teaching to be reliant on controller, choose spore at the two button+joystick stage, the microbe stage teaches how to use a mouse.

I disagree with this theory, because I don't see the correlation between Mario and these enemies.

The psychopath for the Guerillas (which is the enemy referred to in this video, Chained Kongs are a different enemy) are a joke based off of the names of them in the Japanese version. Their Japanese name is ドソキーユング (Dosoki Yungu), which is almost the same name as Donkey Kong's Japanese name ドンキーコング (Donki Kongu), except two of the Katakana characters (ン and コ) were replaced with very similar-looking ones (ソ and ユ). The Japanese psychopath for the Guerilla goes even further by effectively translating into the standard, "This character is a work of fiction. Any resemblance to actual persons is purely coincidental," disclaimer. Guerillas are literally just walking Donkey Kong bootlegs with no connection to the original.

The Chained Kongs, which are stronger variants of the Guerilla found in Barrel Volcano, don't have any revealing information in their psychopaths in either the Japanese or English versions, and only comment about the heat in the volcano.

Since the Guerillas don't have any relation to Donkey Kong, I doubt they'd have any relation to Mario, either. The only connection the two had was the Guerilla's appearance, and since the game itself confirmed that its appearance is coincidental, I don't think there's enough evidence to claim a connection. I'd imagine that the ones who chained them up are more likely to be the Smithy Gang, since Bowyer took control of the Forest Maze and a Guerilla is found in the Smithy Gang-occupied Bowser's Keep throwing barrels in the Trial Course. I'm not sure who put the chains on the Chained Kongs, since the Smithy Gang weren't able to enter Barrel Volcano. The Chained Kongs *do* appear in the Trial Course, though, so... I guess the Smithy Gang managed to capture some?

Color theory for games. Red is often used for indicating danger or injury because its the color of red. Yellow and white is used for navigation because its the color of stars and torch light which travellers used to find their way to towns. Green is an indicator of health because its the color of plants. Blue is often used for magic because its the color of the sky and ocean which are vast and unknowable. Purple is often used for corruption because it stand out against black but is still a dark color (which is used to stand for death and decay) but also because there really isn't a lot of naturally purple anything in nature and it occurs very rarely in nature.

An easier way to explain the Pokédex using length as height is this: Dudunsparce has 2 forms, one with 2 segments and one with 3 segments. The 3 segment is taller than 2 segment in the Pokédex even though they have the same measured height. Thus most long Pokémon like snakes, worms, eels (Or in this case whale balloons) are measured in length.

Now, if they are plant types and do photosynthesize, that would mean that the oxygen produced might be much higher in real life, making the air density much thicker. So, first, we have to check how many grass type pokemon there is. Assuming that the total population of pokemon is equivalent to that of irl animals, then that would be 20,000,121,091,000,000,000 pokemon total. Now, we currently only know about 1021 of these pokemon, so i'll be guessing using the percentage of grass types. Since there's 147 grass types, that roughly gives us 14%. Now, that gives us 2,800,016,952,740,000,000 grass type pokemons. Since the average plant produces roughly 120 ml of oxygen per day, that means that they all produce *336002 km² of oxygen* per day (336,002,034,328,800,000,000 ml). For reference, all the trees in the world make an estimated 360,000,000,000,000 combinde, 933,338× lower than what grass types produce! Now, if trees produce about 28% of all oxygen, that must logicaly mean that theoretically, 1,285,714,285,714,285 ml of oxygen is made each day (1.2 km²). I was trying to figure out the height of my orsimer character in ESO and had started with pixel measurements and a rope texture (with a generous 2-5% margin of error) but once they introduced precision adjustments with a 1 cm scale, with the help of a mod to notate coordinates, I was able to get measurements within 1 cm of accuracy.  Also, orcs in ESO are 226 cm at shortest and 240 cm at tallest -- around 7'5" to 7'10.5" in imperial.  Probably not canonical, but in-game scale can be vastly different compared to real-world or canonical scale, especially in an MMO or other game where you can have a third-person camera (so as not to have a cramped view).

Throwing my own theory in here. I believe Welcome Home is a story about isolation and loneliness, going hand in hand, too, with the mental illness aspect Clown is displaying in these characters. On the website, it makes a comment at one point about how the episodes of Welcome Home from the 70s only had Wally interacting with the audience. He'd go around and learn new lessons, but the other characters were never also trying to teach an audience these things - only Wally. And then the show was taken off the air, and NO ONE remembers it. Wally Darling's puppet is the only puppet found (or they found the design from the original show and re-made it for the exhibit), all of the others have been lost or damaged. Because we mostly see the gang as 2D drawings, we forget that on the show they were entirely puppets, and the 2D aspect was a marketing choice.

So, the puppets are destroyed and lost and the only one left is Wally. On the neighborhood tab where you can click on the houses and read about the characters, Wally (and the secret 'you') is the only one referred to in the present-tense. Everyone else is gone. Wally and House are all alone. I don't think Wally reaching out is trying to be malevolent or creepy - he's been either confirmed as autistic or referenced as being autistic by Clown - he's just been alone for so long, and he wants new friends and somebody, ANYBODY to be with. The entire Welcome Home show is based around all of them being friends and playing together, being together, even if Wally has nothing to say (like in the video clips where we see through his eyes as his friends talk - he just wants to be around them even if he doesn't feel like speaking).

I don't really have an explanation for why the paint makes the Question Answerer mad, but I think Wally appearing in their dreams with the phone, watching and waiting for them to pick it up as it rings endlessly, is just a cry for help. For companionship. For a friend. A friend other than House, from outside the neighborhood. Because, after you spend so long inside your house, you just need to get out.

A few things missed that I think might stand out to help or contest the theory:

- Peshino and Fake Peppino aren't the only clones of Peppino here. In *Peppibot Factory,* one of the levels in the Slums, the *main enemy* is a robot Peppino Robot, clunky in design but still definitely made to copy Peppino.

- There are hidden rooms all over the tower's Floors; not just secrets, but places to sneak in cut content from the final game, such as a *mansion* on Floor 5 that alludes to a much larger family history in the Tower, including origins of boss 1, Pepperman.

- Vigilante isn't quite the mascot of Pizzaboy's, theres an animatronic in that level that is the "Stretcher" seen in the ad. Vigilante has his own lore; he owns the Fun Farm, left behind to him after his grandfather John E. Cheese passed (the farmer cheeseslime seen in some pictures littered throughout the Farm level on floor 2)

- Some of the arcades in *Don't Make A Sound"* are references to defunct or joke concepts for other games, i.e. Pizza Crawler being a dungeon crawling concept that got dropped at some point

- in the finale of the game, you find the original Pillar John holding up the whole tower. If you get all the treasures in the game, you revive him after the tower crumbles and he punches the seemingly-indestructible Pizzahead into the horizon, before celebrating with Gerome the Janitor (the two are presumed family)

As someone with Synesthesia, it definitely sounds a lot cooler than it is. I can only speak for myself, but this has never been an "active" ability for me. I do not choose what senses are mixed together nor when they mix; these are just brain pathways that have always been linked and always proc on the same things consistently. At this point I barely notice because if the smell of pine always produces the sensation of pine pitch between your fingers, then those two things are basically the same sensation. It just becomes part of how you experience things, and like how you don't feel the clothes you're currently wearing, if you focus on it you can feel your shirt and pants but the fact you can feel them really isn't important to actively be aware of.

That said, I think it's interesting you made the Synesthesia connection, because the most common form of Synesthesia is called Grapheme-Color Synesthesia, which is when certain symbols or concepts invoke certain colors within the brain. If you hear statements like "9 is magenta," "the letter "e" is pastel yellow" or "Wednesday is Periwinkle," that's Grapheme-Color Synesthesia (these are all examples of how mine presents). Additionally, there are two categories of Synesthesia; mine is the Associative type, which means when stimulus A happens, I think of something in sense B. This means that while I always ASSOCIATE the number 9 with the color magenta, I do not actively SEE any depiction of a 9 in the color of magenta. That would be the 2nd category: Projector types, in which stimulus A CAUSES sense B to activate in a specific way. Which is to say, if I had Projector-Type Grapheme-Color Synesthesia, it's possible that I may see haybales in a brighter white color than someone without, or see a dark red hue accompanying anyone with a visible weapon; if I was looking for or following someone in particular, I may even see everyone else as being darker or more dull, causing that person to stand out more vibrantly against the city. 

Is it a little convenient and game-ified? Yeah, but it's also not implausible. Again, not an ability that you can "turn on or turn off;" plus, the most universal skill that Synesthesia gives you is the ability to confuse anyone that asks you for a description, because lord knows NOBODY knows what "This tastes purple" means.

A interesting thing about synesthesia is all the different variants that exist.

Colour-Grapheme - This Connects Colours and Characters such as Letters. A may be red for example

Mirror Touch - When You see Someone Move Their Body you feel the same sensations as if you are doing this also

Auditory-Visual - Sounds are Represented as Colours or Words

Visual-Auditory - Colours and Words are Represented as Sounds

Light-Olfactory - Certain Light Levels create Specific scents

Tactition-Olfactory - Smells create physical sensations like a shiver or being touched by another

Lexical-Gustatory - Where Specific Words become Tastes

There are numerous different combinations that when you really think about it mean that we could be experiencing the World in a rather amazing way if learnt.

There is clearly a lot of love poured into it, and I can't imagine how many hours Scott spent reading his own hints and plot points from all the games, making sure they continue making sense even when the entire story is turned on its head. One example of this is the firing notice from FNAF 1. Odor. What was once a mere hint at the presence of bodies inside the animatronics later evolved to be a reference to Michael's scooped, decaying body. And, most peculiarly, it served both purposes. It had set us on track to unravel the first five murders, back when the lore was much simpler, but later evolved with the games, and with us. Same hints played different roles at different points of our collective knowledge, and this is something that makes me unbelievably proud of this series and it's author. I believe that the use of Super Sonic over the years actually had a positive effect on the blue blur. In Sonic 3&K, Sonic can perform an action called the Insta-shield, a move in which Sonic spins so fast that he becomes temporarily invincible, just like his Super form. In Sonic Adventure & Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic would learn how to perform the Light Speed Dash and Light Speed Attack, however by Sonic Heroes it would become part of Sonic’s main actions (sure he would have to learn them again in ‘06 and in Unleashed, but he relearned them again in Generations and Lost World along with his Peel Out ability from CD). In Heroes Sonic could make a giant tornado, this move is similar to his move in Sonic Battle where he could make a smaller twister. Not to mention his Boost ability from Sonic Rush which would carry over to the Modern games starting in Sonic Unleashed. Which finally brings us to Sonic Frontiers, where Sonic’s fighting abilities get an overhaul, not even including the Super form fights against the Titans.

Such as why Waluigi's origins are so obscure: unlike the other main cast who have histories of adventure and action, Waluigi just grew up in a normal construction and demolition family. Which is probably _super_ normal because of how much the Mushroom Kingdom needs to be rebuilt after each of Bowser's attacks. So there really isn't much past to be uncovered for Waluigi in the first place - it's pretty plain.

It also explains why Waluigi has an affinity for both _plants,_ such as Piranha Plants and Wall-Luigi (Mario Strikers Charged) and _technological gear_ such as his frequent use of Bob-ombs, his "Waluigiscopes" from the Olympics and his four-armed backpack (Mario Sports Mix). Construction and demolition have a lot to do with land management, agriculture and machinery, so it makes sense for Waluigi to have skills in those areas if he grew up in a construction-based environment.

How it works is, if something is cancollide false (you can walk through it), then it is rendered invisible when looking through transparent blocks. Several games use this as a mechanic, like platformer-puzzle games.

Hey, So I have been watching all your theories about Minecraft, and it has started me to wonder about the person we play as in the game after all these events have gone down.

As of right now, there are currently nine default skins in the game and are named as follows. Steve, Alex, Zuri, Sunny, Noor, Makena, Kai, Efe and Ari. If we take these skins to mean they are the official characters of Minecraft, then the obvious question becomes where did they come from. You seem to imply with your theories that Steven and the other eight characters are descendants of the ancient builders, but I have a bit of a problem with that, for there is nothing in the game showing where we as the player comes from. Now this could be something that Mojang is planning to add later, like a village full of builder descendants that you came from, but I have two ideas that might actually be more in line to the lore you have presented thus far for Minecraft.

Now idea number one is rather basic, that being that Steve and the others are all children of villagers who for whatever reason are born with both the resemblance and the gifts of the ancient builders, and thus they were sent off on a grand adventure to discover the secrets of their peoples long lost past. This idea though I admit is weak, as one it would have to be an extremely rare chance for such a thing to happen, but not so unlikely that you didn't run into others like yourself in the world.

Idea number two is where I'm putting my money, for this idea involves the Illigers, and the theory you presented that the Illigers are trying to bring back the ancient Builders via dark magic, for I think that they succeeded in bringing a builder back to life, and that builder is your player character.

Now two questions of course arise from this idea, one being that if you are a builder resurrected by the Illagers, why do they attack you, followed by why are there not more of you out in the world. Both questions are actually easy to answer, for I think that not only were the Illigers wanting to bring builders back to life, but given the fact that they hold sway over the other creations they have at their disposal, I think they also wanted to control these resurrected builders. But for whatever reason, they couldn't control you, and later you were somehow able to escape from their clutches before they could kill you and start over with their experiments, explaining why Illagers would want to kill you on sight, while also explaining why there are no others like you, because they are afraid that like with you, the others they might create will not be able to be controlled, thus escaping and later messing with their plans just like you inevitably do if you survive long enough in Minecraft, after all, only you seem capable of repelling a Illager raid on the Villagers.

But its all just speculation on my part at this point, though I would love to see you tackle this idea in one of your videos if it holds merit.

I really like the theories but I think I need to point out that the third one has an issue. As an artist I can tell you that when you work on a big illustration/digital painting like the one that teases the dlc, some if not most professionals will start the colouring process by working in black and white to set the values of the piece in place. Only later will they work with actually color. Color theory is kinda hard to explain, but work with me here.

My theory is that the artist left her in black and white because she stands out more without color and the character's actual color palette might distract more than help the piece. For example if her color palette is on the warm side she wouldn't stand out as much as she does against the golden Freddy statue.

It might also be a question of how the colour in that environment would behave. For example something like warm grey in a bright red background won't be perceived as grey but as a blue-ish color. Sometimes the real color and the color we perceive it to be, isn't the same. I think that maybe this was a way for the artist to stylise this phenomena, taking advantage of the cooler feel that the grey gives the character contrasting with the warmth of the statue

So you know how everywhere around the factory there appears to be large holes in the walls, cracks, or even splits in the ground and train tracks? 

My theory is that Bron is the toy responsible for such destruction. We already get an idea on the pure size and density/weight of the Bron toy model in the rejected toys room. We need a large mechanical claw to even move the Bron toys. Not only that but the Bron Toys appear to be really hard and dense compared to the soft bodied Huggy Wuggy or the elastic Mommy Long Legs. 

Huggy Wuggy like Kissy Missy have such soft bodies they struggle to even pull levers. But this also allows them to fit into tight spaces like air vents. But their heads must be hard because that’s ultimately what they use to bite and eat us. I think Huggy Wuggy headbutts the vent doors to get in or to break out and get us towards the end of the game. Mommy Long Legs on the other hand has a hard and round torso, which allows players to escape her by jumping into small holes in the walls or ground. But she has extremely long reach which allows her to climb to high heights and scale up walls. 

If we also take into account that the toys usually stay in their respective stations/areas, we see that Huggy is mainly at the entrance with the role of obedient security guard. (He guards the entrance and provides a security key). Mommy is the care taker of children in the game center as well as caretaker of the other toys/experiments (she might have even been caring for the Prototype but she definitely was caring for Pugapillar, Bunzo Bunny, and the small Huggy Wuggies. She must have also been caring for Poppy, or at least making sure she stayed locked up.) so Mommy’s role was a caretaker but she does have violent outbursts which is why she  punished Bunzo Bunny and the small Huggy Wuggies when they fail. As a care taker, she also delivered children to their tests and the children who fail she would punish/lecture like a real mom would. 

Going along with this trend, what would be Bron’s role? I think given the size and density of his body and his cutout that shows him holding a construction sign/in a railway cart, I want to say Bron was something of a groundskeeper. Due to his size, he had to use the railways to travel around the factory since his large and heavy body would be hard enough to break walls and floors. If something needed to be built, torn down, or something heavy needed to be lifted up high, Bron would be the experiment to use for those tasks. He may have also been tasked with collecting and delivering broken or rejected toys(or trash) using the railway and Barry the train cart. But he would be dedicated to the railway system in order for him to get to places quickly around the factory and without accidentally breaking structures. He is essentially a living crane/wrecking ball. Again, this is based off the size and density of the rejected Bron toys. This would explain why there are so many broken walls, a place abandoned for 10 years wouldn’t really have such destruction, I mean it looks like an earthquake happened. But I think Bron started roaming around the factory without the rail station, causing the destruction and for floors that can not support his weight to collapse. I also think that Barry was his friend that he was protecting by locking Barry away in a safe spot of the railways. But the players killed Barry to open an area, so Bron will come after us because of that.

Okay, learning that there are TWO spirit-infused like materials in this universe is very interesting to me, Remnant and Agony. What is interesting to me is it seems to follow the concept in the paranormal world of there being (maybe of many) two types of haunting. For me, it reads that Remnant, being the soul of the one who has died, is much like a physical possession, the common idea that the soul or spirit itself of the one who died is inhabiting an object. But Agony for me reads like the Stone-Tape Theory. The Stone-Tape Theory postulates that in the presence of a traumatic (or extremely-emotional) event, the emotions and energy that the event produce is recorded onto the surroundings, thus the Stone * Taping those emotions and storing them. (I myself subscribe more to the Stone-Tape theory as to why hauntings occur.) Whether this was intentional or not, it's very impressive that the lore has shaped out to be this way!

The use of poppy plants in the revival experiments also has some interesting ecological and historical basis. This is because poppy’s are a pioneer species that rejuvenates the soil of areas destroyed by man made or natural disasters, increasing the ecological capacity of said region. This historical basis to this comes from World War One, where the barren fields of No-man’s land became home to thousands of poppy plants, becoming such reoccurring sighting that the poppy flower itself became a symbol of remembrance towards those who have died in the war.

See, it’s important to note that the only ender dragon we ever see is a female, as shown by our prize once defeating the dragon: an egg. "Is there such a thing as a modern broom?"

Well, yes.  Most modern brooms are made with synthetic bristles, extruded plastic in the shape of pieces of straw.  Go back a generation or two, and you get a straw broom, like the ones you can still buy in stores if you know where to shop.  But go back even farther, and a broom is a stick with twigs tied to it.

The ancestor of the modern rake.

As for the pie theory, I have my doubts. If she was going to do that, why not turn the groom into pies, rather than scare him off and risk him coming back?  It would be more permanent and more profitable.  No, I suspect the pie filling is a cherry-red herring, at least in that regard.

Likewise, the knives don't tie in by serial killer standards.  Serial killers have fetishization of their killing methods.  The infamous Ed Gein, for example, had one set of skinning tools for all of his victims.  It becomes a part of their identity -- for them to change instruments or devices would be like you suddenly making a video series on beekeeping.  The knives must be a key to something else.

Tian li 天理 is actually a phrase that exists in chinese, used in longer phrases like :天理难容 (Tian li nan rong) (something along the lines of Order would not allow). It's... less destiny and more natural order, like physics, but imposed upon this world. Like karma, or things like balance. Basically, rules of the world. In Genshin, it is hinted that the rules of the world is opressive and similar to dictatorship. 
By arrogation in the original terms, they meant less taking something, and more that humans have advanced to a technological level they should not have, this is how how powerful humans should be, and therefore they shall be destroyed. Part of the reason Khanriah was destroyed was that Gold, the alchemist, figured out how to create life. And that is a power the principles determines that humans are not meant to have. And for the achievement of one man, the entire kingdom was destroyed. Of course there was also the matter that the things Gold created were monsters and they were out of control, but still.
There's also a theory in CN that Visions, or in CN, Eye(s) of the God(s), are used to spy on those Celestia deem dangerous. It makes sense from the original text. These are the Eyes of the Gods, they're given by Celestia and not the Archons, given to those with the power to become gods and binds them to their wish so they become so vulnerable when their Visions were lost. Of course, this is just a working theory somewhere.
Much like how in some literature Celestia would be used as a name for a personification or a god/goddess, 天理 can also be used as a name. In fact in the CN fandom it is often seen as and referred to as a name/ title.

Regarding Glamrock Bonnie, technology has advanced far enough to give animatronics sentience and personality, but Freddy clearly states in SB that it's not possible for any of the animatronics to harm anyone or anything, as it goes against their programming. 

Because Bonnie's parts were needed to revive Afton, Bonnie became the unfortunate test subject of the glitchtrap virus. He was manipulated into going to (and getting scrapped in) Monty Golf because Afton needed a scapegoat, something to throw everyone off his scent. With the test successful, Afton gave Vanny the go-ahead to gradually unleash the virus system-wide. 

As for Cassidy being the princess, that makes way more sense than Vanessa being the princess. However, I do not believe the so-called Princess Quest ending is the true ending to the game and it's only there as a form of symbolism.

I saw a theory a while back about Bonnie's absence that I can't stop thinking about. The person theorized that Monty didn't destroy Bonnie because he wandered into Gator Golf, but that Bonnie *purposely* went looking for Monty and destroyed him, thus getting *himself* decommissioned. Think about it, Bonnie is one of the most aggressive animatronics in the FNAF series, I believe he was the first one to come looking for you in FNAF 1, he has a pattern of being aggressive. I also think that if Monty destroyed Bonnie he would've been the one that got scrapped and Bonnie would still be around, but because *Bonnie* was the one to go and destroy Monty, he was the one that was done away with.

 I don't know, that theory makes more sense to me personally because I can't see any other reason why Bonnie would be scrapped, he's too popular. If he was destroyed, they could just put him back together again, right? But if he was the aggressor in that scenario...maybe not so much. Maybe he needed to be scrapped to prevent future incidents.

Plus it's also a bit humorous when you think about it, because if Bonnie *was* the one to destroy Monty and get himself decommissioned, from that point on Monty decided he was going to be the aggressor, couldn't let anyone know that Bonnie got the drop on him.

But hey, that's just a theory.....
